name: Emotional Awareness and Expression Therapy (EAET)
url: https://unlearnyourpain.com/product/eaet-emotional-awareness-and-expression-therapy-for-chronic-pain/ (no official standalone site; eaet.org is an unrelated ed-tech conference; lab: https://s.wayne.edu/lumleylab/)
founders: Mark A. Lumley, PhD (Distinguished Professor of Psychology, Wayne State University)
Howard Schubiner, MD (internist; Mind Body Medicine Center, Ascension Providence, Southfield MI; Michigan State University)
founded_year_range: 2008-2012. Precursor trials ran 2006-2011 (affective self-awareness, Hsu 2010). The NIAMS R01 AR057808 trial first called it 'Emotional Exposure Therapy'. Manual v2 used the EAET name by Sept 2012. The name first appeared in a paper in 2016 (Burger).
cost_summary: No program fee. Patients pay standard psychotherapy fees, roughly USD 100-250 per session, so about USD 1,000-2,500 for a typical 9-session course (author estimate). Treatment manuals are free online. Clinician training costs USD 600 (5 x 3-hr Zoom sessions, 15 CE via Wayne State; unlearnyourpain.com, Oct 2026; waitlist only). The Unlearn Your Pain workbook costs about USD 25.
mechanisms: neuroplastic/learned pain (brain-generated danger signal / predictive processing)
limbic system impairment / amygdala threat conditioning
mechanism_summary: EAET holds that the brain generates or amplifies primary/centralized pain and other somatic symptoms. Lifetime trauma, adversity and interpersonal or intrapsychic conflict sensitize a brain "danger/alarm" system. Avoidance of primary emotions ("affect phobia") keeps that system active: chiefly anger tied to agency and assertion, plus guilt, grief and longing tied to attachment. Symptoms are expected to resolve through three processes. Patients re-attribute pain to the brain and emotion. They undergo experiential exposure to the avoided emotions, which works as a corrective emotional experience or "memory reconsolidation". They practise adaptive assertive and connecting expression in real relationships. One mechanism is applied across fibromyalgia, IBS, pelvic pain, MUS/SSD, musculoskeletal pain and headache. Patients with high trauma or conflict loads are expected to be the best candidates.
techniques: pain-attribution education (brain, not tissue, generates pain), with emotion-symptom demonstrations
life-stress interview linking stressors to symptom onset
experiential emotional exposure: empty-chair talk to an imagined offender in the present tense
anger expression with voice, face and body, including imagined protective or retaliatory action
sequenced processing: anger, then guilt, then sadness/grief/longing, then self-compassion and letting go
rescripting memories; current self comforting the younger self
unsent letters read aloud; expressive writing at home
assertive and connecting communication: role play, then real-life practice
experiential challenge of probability overestimation and catastrophizing
self-forgiveness and forgiving or letting go of others
homework: engaging avoided behaviors and relationships; guided visualization audio
standard dose: 1 individual + 8 x 90-min small-group sessions (5-7 patients); also 3-session individual, single 90-min interview, 2-hr class, 10-module internet versions
mainstream_notes: The 2019 HHS Pain Management Best Practices Inter-Agency Task Force report lists EAET as a behavioral treatment option (section 2.5, p. 38, verified in the report). Funding has come from NIH and the VA. NIAMS funded the fibromyalgia RCT. NIH funds the 4-arm M&M trial (CBT vs ACT vs EAET vs control; Rush/Wayne State; NCT06044649; 408 enrolled). The VA funded the Yarns trials. VA Greater Los Angeles delivers EAET clinically and by telehealth. A multisite NCCIH-funded pragmatic trial in veterans (UCLA lead; NCT07218757; estimated N=672) began recruiting in January 2026. Academic programs at Wayne State, Michigan, Stanford, UCLA, Stockholm/Karolinska, Toronto and Utah. Not named in NICE or the VA/DoD pain guidelines. Training is run by the developers.
insurance_notes: There is no EAET-specific code or coverage policy. When a licensed clinician delivers it, it is billed as standard psychotherapy (90832/90834/90837, group 90853) or as a health-behavior intervention (96158/96164). Many private mind-body therapists who offer EAET are cash-pay or out-of-network.

key_trials.citation: Lumley MA, Schubiner H, et al. Pain 2017;158:2354-2363 (PMID 28796118)
key_trials.design: Cluster RCT (40 groups); EAET vs CBT vs FM education; 8 x 90-min group sessions
key_trials.finding: EAET did not beat education on the primary outcome (pain severity at 6 months). It did beat education on most secondary outcomes (d 0.29-0.45) and on 'much improved' (34.8% vs 15.4%). Against CBT it was similar on most outcomes but better on widespread pain and on the rate of 50% pain reduction (22.5% vs 8.3%).

key_trials.citation: Yarns BC, Jackson NJ, Alas A, Melrose RJ, Lumley MA, Sultzer DL. JAMA Netw Open 2024;7:e2415842 (PMID 38869899)
key_trials.design: RCT, EAET vs CBT, older veterans with musculoskeletal pain; 1 individual + 8 group sessions
key_trials.finding: EAET beat CBT on pain severity post-treatment (-1.59) and at 6 months (-1.01). At least 30% pain reduction: 63% vs 17%. At least 50%: 35% vs 7%. EAET was also better on anxiety, depression, PTSD and life satisfaction.

key_trials.citation: Yarns BC, et al. Pain Med 2020;21:2811-2822 (PMID 32451528)
key_trials.design: Preliminary RCT, EAET vs CBT, older veterans
key_trials.finding: EAET produced lower pain severity than CBT post-treatment and at 3 months (partial eta2 0.13-0.16). 41.7% of EAET patients had at least 30% pain reduction, vs one CBT patient.

key_trials.citation: Thakur ER, et al. Neurogastroenterol Motil 2017;29:e13143 (PMID 28643436)
key_trials.design: RCT, EAET vs relaxation vs waitlist; 3 individual sessions; IBS
key_trials.finding: At 10 weeks, EAET (but not relaxation) reduced IBS symptom severity vs waitlist. Both improved quality of life. EAET did not reduce psychological symptoms; relaxation reduced depression.

key_trials.citation: Ziadni MS, et al. Health Psychol 2018;37:282-290 (PMID 29154608)
key_trials.design: RCT, single 90-min EAET interview vs TAU; primary-care medically unexplained symptoms
key_trials.finding: At 6 weeks, lower pain severity, pain interference, sleep problems and psychological symptoms.

key_trials.citation: Carty JN, et al. Pain Med 2019;20:1321-1329 (PMID 30252113)
key_trials.design: RCT, single life-stress EAET interview vs TAU; women with chronic urogenital pain
key_trials.finding: Lower pain severity and pelvic-floor symptoms. No effect on interference or on anxiety and depression.

key_trials.citation: Maroti D, Lumley MA, Schubiner H, et al. J Psychosom Res 2022;163:111068 (PMID 36327532)
key_trials.design: RCT, 10-week internet EAET vs waitlist; somatic symptom disorder
key_trials.finding: Somatic symptoms fell at post-treatment and 4-month follow-up. Gains in pain, depression, anxiety and insomnia were not retained. About 20% had substantial improvement.

key_trials.citation: Krohner S, Town J, Cannoy CN, Schubiner H, Rapport LJ, Grekin E, Lumley MA. J Pain 2024;25:39-52 (PMID 37479050)
key_trials.design: RCT, single 90-min emotion-focused psychodynamic video interview (EAET/ISTDP-based variant) vs waitlist; musculoskeletal pain plus at least 3 adverse childhood experiences
key_trials.finding: No effect on pain severity. Pain interference fell (partial eta2 0.05), and pain attributions and controllability shifted.

key_trials.citation: Maroti D, Ljungdahl M, Petersen H, Rööst M, Lumley MA, Falkenström F, Lilliengren P. Internet Interv 2026;44:100942 (PMID 41969788)
key_trials.design: RCT, guided vs unguided internet EAET (10 modules); persistent physical symptoms
key_trials.finding: Both arms improved, with no significant group x time difference. Post-treatment d was -0.21 favouring guidance. Responders: 47.2% guided vs 29.6% unguided. Differences attenuated at follow-up. There was no inactive control.

key_trials.citation: Hsu MC, Schubiner H, Lumley MA, et al. J Gen Intern Med 2010;25:1064-70 (PMID 20532650)
key_trials.design: RCT of the precursor 'affective self-awareness' intervention vs waitlist; fibromyalgia
key_trials.finding: At 6 months, 45.8% vs 0% had at least 30% pain reduction. Physical function and tender-point threshold also improved.

key_trials.citation: Slavin-Spenny O, Lumley MA, et al. Ann Behav Med 2013;46:181-92 (PMID 23620190)
key_trials.design: RCT, precursor anger awareness and expression training vs relaxation vs waitlist; headache
key_trials.finding: Anger training was roughly equal to relaxation; both beat waitlist on some headache outcomes. This was a precursor, not the branded protocol.

key_trials.citation: Kaufmann D, Sturgeon JA, ..., Yarns BC, ..., Lumley MA. Pain Med 2026;27:948-951 (PMID 41761583)
key_trials.design: Preliminary RCT, migraine (brief report; NCT05837650, 30 enrolled)
key_trials.finding: Published, but no abstract is available on PubMed. The results are unverified.

controversy:
Concerns include:
- Nearly all trials are developer-affiliated, with no fully independent replication. The Stockholm I-EAET group is partly independent, but Lumley co-authors. Lumley discloses EAET training fees and CognifiSense fees. Schubiner owns Mind Body Publishing.
- The trials are unblinded and often use waitlist or TAU controls.
- The largest RCT (fibromyalgia 2017) missed its primary outcome against education, and the adversity-interview RCT missed pain severity.
- Effects on anxiety and depression are inconsistent.
- The CBT arm in Yarns 2024 had an unusually low response rate (17%).
- The practitioner guide endorses intense anger expression, including imagined violent retaliation against abusers, which raises acceptability and retraumatization questions.
- "Memory reconsolidation" and "danger/alarm circuit" claims have not been tested mechanistically.
- Like other mind-body pain models, it risks a psychogenic framing that patients may reject if extended to ME/CFS or long COVID.
- Press framing of it as a "new gold standard" goes beyond what the evidence shows.

Randomized trials published (EAET or close variants)

Listed as a behavioral treatment option in the HHS Pain Management Best Practices Task Force report (p. 38)
NPR Shots feature on a fibromyalgia patient treated with EAET

indicators.metric: Media spike after JAMA Netw Open trial
indicators.value: Covered by UCLA Health, ScienceDaily, HealthDay, McKnight's and MDedge ('new psychotherapeutic gold standard')
USD 600 Zoom course; waitlist only; next cohort dates given inconsistently (autumn 2026 vs early 2027)
No dedicated subreddit or app; only incidental mentions in PRT/Sarno communities

popularity.reach_estimate: About 10^4 people. Trial participants total about 1,500. Several hundred to low thousands of clinicians have been trained, each treating a few to dozens of patients. VA and academic clinics add to this. Readers of Schubiner's books (likely tens of thousands) were not counted as EAET recipients.
popularity.method_notes:
The trajectory is anchored on documented milestones, not usage data:
- precursor trials, 2006-2011
- R01 manual, 2012
- first EAET-named paper, 2016
- Pain and NGM RCTs, 2017
- HHS listing, NPR story and review, 2019
- VA pilot and internet versions, 2020-2022
- This Might Hurt / PPDA attention, 2023
- JAMA Netw Open trial and media spike, 2024
- multisite NCCIH pragmatic trial launch and new trials, 2025-2026
Google Trends volume for EAET is too low to be informative, and the acronym collides with other uses. There are no user counts or app metrics. Reach is a rough order-of-magnitude estimate built from trial Ns and assumed training throughput.
